tagline: River, road and excursion trains share the steep Nantahala Gorge.
intro: The Nantahala Byway moves from agricultural bottomlands into a deep, steep-walled gorge, with the Blue Ridge Mountains as its backdrop. Two-lane US 19/74 follows the river, with picnic areas along the way. NCDOT presents this state scenic byway as a drive of changing river, farm and mountain views; its guide gives 47.2 miles and a driving time of one hour, ten minutes.

At the western end, the highway changed the journey through Andrews in 1979, when a new four-lane road opened and the old alignment through town became US 19 Business. The byway now takes that Main Street route before rejoining US 74. Through the gorge, the Great Smoky Mountains Railroad runs parallel to the highway, giving this river passage a second way to travel. The excursion operation began in 1988, after investors secured a lease on the former Murphy Branch just 48 hours before Norfolk Southern planned to send work trains to dismantle the track.

Start at Marble and continue through Andrews to Topton, then follow US 74/19 toward Bryson City. Wesser lies along US 74 between Hewitt and Almond, where excursion trains stop. After Bryson City, the byway continues across the Tuckasegee River and via Ela Road to Highway 19A, ending at US 74.
notice: The railroad parallels US 74 through the gorge, with occasional glimpses from the byway.

moments.title: Marble
moments.text: Marble’s quarries sent most of their stone out as cemetery headstones across nine states. They opened in 1902, shipping Regal Blue and Confederate Gray marble on the Southern Railway’s Murphy Branch. The stone also went into the Cherokee County Courthouse, built in 1926 and constructed entirely of marble. By 1946, heavy water flow and excessive jointing had closed all but one quarry. None now operates, and all have filled with water. The community’s former name, Marble Springs, survives in the name of its Baptist church on Marble Road. Airport Road follows the former US 19 alignment through Marble, replaced in 1979.

moments.title: Wesser
moments.text: At Wesser, the lower rafting run meets a former railway whistle stop. The eight-mile run from the Nantahala Powerhouse to Wesser has Class II and III rapids. Its water depends on releases from Nantahala Lake: water diverted through a 5.5-mile penstock passes through the powerhouse before returning to the river channel. Beyond the main take-out, Lower Nantahala Falls, also called Wesser Falls, drops at about 45 degrees among sharp rocks. Excursion trains on the Great Smoky Mountains Railroad stop in Wesser. The Appalachian Trail crosses the river on a bridge beside the Nantahala Outdoor Center.

moments.title: Bryson City
moments.text: Main and Everett streets preserve the T-shaped layout of a county seat first called Charleston. The town changed its name to Bryson City in 1889 to recognize Thaddeus Bryson’s part in its development and avoid confusion with Charleston, South Carolina. Southern Railway’s depot followed in 1895, a frame building with broad eaves and wooden ornament. Passenger service ended in 1948. After North Carolina bought the Murphy Branch in 1988, the station was refurbished for excursion passengers. Trains now depart for the Nantahala Gorge and Tuckasegee River. The depot stands at Everett and Fry streets in the downtown area.
